citations.narrative:
A non-human primate suffered an injury while being handled for a sedation procedure. On 1/15/26, the tip of the 3rd digit
on the left foot of a female cynomolgus macaque (EQ474) became entrapped between the floor and squeeze back cage.
The injury required treatment by a partial toe amputation of the last 2 phalanges of that digit. Animals that are not handled
carefully can become injured and distressed. Handling of all animals shall be done as expeditiously and carefully as
possible in a manner that does not cause trauma, overheating, excessive cooling, behavioral stress, physical harm, or
unnecessary discomfort. Correct from 4/14/26 forward.

Primary enclosures in the facility do not protect the non-human primates from injury. Between August and November
2025 multiple non-human primates became entrapped and/or sustained injuries due to the design of their enclosures.
On 9/21/25, 1 Cynomolgus Macaque infant (T25047) sustained trauma after extending its right arm under the guillotine
door between enclosures. A neighboring macaque was able to manipulate the locked door to allow a small crack under
the door through which the arm was extended. The infant’s arm was broken and required amputation.
On 11/05/25, the right leg of a female Cynomolgus Macaque (EW268) became entrapped in the squeeze-back portion of
her cage. The cage had previously been sent for repair, but a bar had not been rewelded back on the cage properly.
Despite treatment, it was observed that she had a lack of motor function and sensation in the foot so a mid-femoral
amputation was performed on 12/5/25.
Between 8/29-9/22/25, 5 Cynomolgus Macaques became entrapped in their cages while in quarantine. Each animal was
able to get an arm caught in the bottom of their cage, resulting in redness and swelling of the affected limb. Each animal
was sedated and freed from the cage and received analgesics and cold compresses to reduce pain and swelling in the
affected limbs.
Animals who are injured or entangled by their primary enclosure may experience pain, injury, stress, and even death.
Correct by ensuring that enclosures protect nonhuman primates from injury. Corrected prior to date of inspection on
4/14/26
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
Additional Inspectors:
Lindsay Livingston, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
